title: Duplication as a trend series — adopt, and counting what

dims.name: The verdict
dims.question: Does duplication become a series, a gate, or nothing?
dims.problem: This repository sorts every automated check into one of two kinds. A gate blocks a merge or a deploy. A trend is a number that reaches a person and blocks nothing. The rule that sorts them is `docs/spec/gate-or-trend.md`. Duplication is a candidate check. This row picks its kind, and refusal is a permitted answer.

opts.label: A trend series. The number reaches the maintainer and blocks nothing.
A gate. A duplication level above a threshold turns a build red.
Nothing. Record the refusal in docs/gates.md, Not gated deliberately.
opts.src: #228 Destination — refusal is a first-class result

opts.label: Decide after a formatter and a linter land, because both change the tree.

dims.name: Teeth
dims.question: Does a duplication number ever refuse anything?
dims.problem: A trend usually refuses nothing. This repository made one exception. Two complexity series carry a per-scope cap in `stryker.floors.json`. The cap is the highest value the repository already reached, and `pnpm deploy:site` refuses when a capped scope exceeds it. The spec caps the two counts that rise only when somebody writes worse code. It leaves uncapped the two that rise with any new code at all. This row asks which side a duplication count sits on.

opts.label: No cap. The number is read, and it refuses nothing anywhere.
A per-scope cap in the floors file, which pnpm deploy:site refuses against.
Ship cap entries as unarmed now, and decide arming after the window fills.
Cap it today, at whatever the first measurement reports.

dims.name: What the record carries
dims.question: Which numbers land in the record, and what stamps their meaning?
dims.problem: A trend record is a line of numbers written each run. Two properties decide whether it can be compared to its own past. First, the shape: a count or a share. Second, a hash of every input that changes the number, stamped beside it. The complexity series already carries such a hash, named `fixtureHash`, over the ESLint version and the rule options. A duplication number has its own inputs: the jscpd version, the token threshold, the line threshold and the detection mode.

opts.label: Three counts per population, and a duplication hash separate from fixtureHash.
The duplication percentage, which is the number jscpd prints.
Fold the jscpd inputs into the existing fixtureHash, so one hash covers both tools.
opts.src: #237 session — the floors file already reads one fixtureHash

opts.label: Record the number with no hash beside it, and trust the pinned versions.

dims.name: Deliberate near-repetition
dims.question: What happens to the clones this repository wrote on purpose?
dims.problem: Some repeated code here is intentional. Two TypeScript interfaces share a field vocabulary across the adapter boundary by design. One pair of functions is `mirrored` because a spec says so. A duplication tool reports all of them. This row decides what the measurement does about that: it can suppress them in the source, it can tune the threshold past them, or it can leave them in the number.

opts.label: Leave them in the number. Name them once in the baseline, and read movement.
Put jscpd:ignore-start blocks around each intentional clone in the source.
Raise the token threshold until the intentional clones stop reporting.
State no rule. Whoever reads the series judges each clone at the time.

dims.name: How an ignore block is watched
dims.question: If the source can suppress a clone, what sees the suppression?
dims.problem: A `jscpd:ignore-start` block removes its lines from the duplicated count and from the total line count at the same time. The share does not move, and the count falls. The comment lives in a source file, far from any configuration a deploy inspects. This repository has met that exact shape before with a different tool, and it built a gate for it. This row decides whether it builds the same thing again.

opts.label: A declared count per population, swept from source by a gate at merge. Links are generated, never stored.
The declaration stores a permanent code link for each block, reviewed in the diff.
Each block becomes its own recorded series, labelled by file and line.
opts.src: #237 session, considered so the reason to refuse it is written down

opts.label: Allow the directive and watch nothing. Review catches it, or nobody does.

dims.name: Which populations
dims.question: Over which files does the tool run, and in how many runs?
dims.problem: Every other series here is counted per scope. A scope is one glob in `stryker.scopes.json`, and there are eight. Duplication differs from complexity in one way that matters. Complexity is a property of one function. A clone is a relation between two places, and the two places can sit in different scopes, or in code no scope declares at all. So the shape of the population is a real choice, not a detail.

opts.label: One run over the eight scopes together. Count a clone in each scope it touches.
Eight runs, one per scope. The eight numbers sum to a total.
opts.src: complexity spec §2, one population per glob

opts.label: The eight scopes, and gates/ as a ninth population.
One number for the whole repository, with no scope split at all.
The whole tree, TypeScript files only. No scope list, and no data files.
opts.src: #237 session, from the owner's whole-tree proposal

opts.label: The eight scopes for the cap, and one whole-tree TypeScript number no scope list can shrink.
opts.src: #237 session, answering the owner's blind-spot concern

verdict-series.why: Duplication passes clause B of the sorting rule without argument: the population excludes test files, so no assertion moves the number. It fails clause A, because the remedy for a high level is a refactor and not a finite diff.
rel: A series that cannot be compared to its own past is a flat line with noise on it.
docs/spec/gate-or-trend.md §2 — a trend's characteristic failure is silence that looks like health
notes: Clause A is arguable here, and the spec says what to do about that. jscpd names the exact file and line range of both halves of a clone, which looks like a named remedy. gate-or-trend.md §1 states that a candidate which passes clause B and is argued through clause A is suspect rather than classified. Trend is the classification that survives that instruction.

The source that put duplication on this map: SlopCodeBench, March 2026, found duplication rose in 89.8% of agent runs against flat human baselines. One study, unreplicated. It motivates the series and proves nothing about this repository.

verdict-gate.why: jscpd ships a --threshold flag that exits 1 above a duplication percentage, so a gate is one flag away. The map's routing ticket found that style rules may gate, which invites the question here.
rel: Three of twelve clones here are intentional, so a threshold reddens a build for a design decision.
#232 — two parallel interfaces plus one spec-mandated mirror, read by hand
A gate needs a number to breach, so it cannot run without a threshold.
notes: #229 routed this ticket explicitly: duplication produces a count rather than a complaint, so it sorts by the older gate-or-trend rule and not by the new stranger standard.

verdict-refuse.why: The map names refusal as a first-class result. docs/gates.md already holds eight refusals in its Not gated deliberately section, so the verdict has a home.
rel: A refused candidate writes no record, so no hash and no counts exist.
A refused candidate produces no number, so there is nothing to cap or to leave uncapped.
A refused candidate reads no source, so no directive exists to sweep for.
notes: The honest case for it: the repository already carries 45 gates and eight series. Each new number costs a nightly step, a freshness bound and a row somebody keeps true.
The case against it: this is the one signal the only trajectory study of agent-written code found more consistent than complexity, and complexity is already measured here.

verdict-later.why: A formatter and a linter both change the tree. A duplication baseline taken before either lands describes a tree that will not exist.
rel: A deferred candidate writes no record now, so no hash is defined.
notes: It is weaker than it looks. jscpd tokenizes, so whitespace and quote style do not move its number. #231 measured the reformat diff at 348 files, and none of that diff changes a token stream.
A linter that removes real duplication does move the number. That is a code change, and a series exists to see code changes.

teeth-uncapped.why: No cap. The number is read and it refuses nothing. This was the position before the owner's override, and its stated reason does not survive inspection.
rel: Without a stamped hash a movement cannot be told from a re-measurement under new parameters.
docs/spec/complexity-on-the-trend-layer.md §4 — a record under a different counting rule is refused, not compared
notes: The reason given for this cell was wrong, and the correction is why the position moved. It read: duplicated lines grows with the codebase legitimately, so a cap refuses a feature. That is the complexity spec's test for `complexity-functions` and `complexity-mass`, and duplication fails it. A clean new feature adds zero duplicated lines. Duplication rises only when somebody writes duplication, which is `complexity-mass-over-10`'s property, and that series is capped.

Legitimate growth still happens, and it is occasional. #232 found two of twelve clones are parallel type declarations by design. The floors file already answers that: a deliberate rise costs a `notes` entry, exactly as it does for a genuinely complex function.
The second reason for this cell was real. The Watching row closes it by measurement rather than by argument.

teeth-capped.why: The floors file already carries cap machinery, and CAPPED_SERIES is a list a name can join. A cap derived from the repository's own history asks nothing until the repository shows what it holds.
rel: A cap compares a stored number to a new one, so both must carry the same stamped hash.
scripts/lib/floors.ts — the floors file refuses when fixtureHash differs from the record's label
Arming today means arming over a level nobody has calibrated, and over a route down nothing watches.
notes: Clause A is met more cleanly here than for complexity. jscpd prints both halves of the clone, so the remedy names two file ranges rather than a whole function.
The cost is a second hash ingredient. fixtureHash covers ESLint and its rule options only, so a duplication cap needs its own hash or the two tools' calibrations couple.

teeth-arm-later.why: Cap entries ship `unarmed` with their date, and arming waits for the calibration window to fill. The floors file already parses this state, so the decision is written down without being taken.
rel: An unarmed cap still reads a record, so the hash must exist before arming.
scripts/lib/floors.ts — parseCap accepts the unarmed sentinel with a date
A cap that plans to arm needs the route around it watched before that day.
#237 session — an ignore block moves the clone count and the denominator together, so an unwatched cap falls silently
notes: The cost, unchanged by anything here: an unarmed cap entry is a line that reads as protection and refuses nothing. `docs/gates.md` exists to refuse exactly that shape. What makes it acceptable is that the file states `unarmed` explicitly, rather than carrying a number nobody chose.

record-counts.why: Three counts per population: clones found, duplicated lines, and total lines. The page derives the share. A duplication hash covers the jscpd version, the token threshold, the line threshold and the mode.
notes: The fixture that pins the tool is the same shape as the complexity inventory: a pair of files with a known clone, and the expected clone count and token count written beside them. A jscpd upgrade that retokenizes then turns red rather than moving every series at once.
The hash stays separate from fixtureHash on purpose. A shared hash makes an ESLint upgrade refuse every duplication record, and the two tools share no input.

record-ratio.why: The percentage is what jscpd prints and what a reader asks for first. It is one number instead of three.
rel: A share falls when the tree grows, so a fixed set of intentional clones reads as improvement.
notes: The arithmetic: #232 measured 133 duplicated lines in 25,999, which is 0.51%. Add five thousand clean lines and the same 133 reads 0.43%.

The complexity prototype put every candidate ratio through two gaming moves and no ratio survived both. The record carries counts and the page derives shares, one step earlier than mutation-score being spelled killed over total.

record-shared-hash.why: One hash is one thing to keep true. The floors file already reads a single fixtureHash, so nothing new is parsed.
rel: A shared hash makes an ESLint upgrade refuse duplication records that no ESLint input touched.
notes: The complexity hash is documented as the ESLint version, the parser version, the rule options and the inventory totals. jscpd reads none of them.

record-unhashed.why: package.json can pin jscpd exactly, and the thresholds can live in one checked-in config. A hash then restates what two files already say.
rel: One threshold step moved the identical tree from 12 clones to 82, so an unstamped number is not comparable.
#232 — jscpd defaults 50/5 gave 12 clones and 0.51%; 20/3 gave 82 clones and 2.51%
notes: The complexity series answered this already. A pinned version states an intention and node_modules states a fact, and only the fact is an input to the number.

deliberate-in-the-level.why: The intentional clones stay in the count. They are named once when the baseline is recorded. This was the position before the owner's override.
notes: It still works, and it is now the weaker of the two. A note in a baseline document has no anchor in the source, so it drifts as the code moves and nothing reports the drift.
It also gives up the reason. #232's by-hand pass established which clones are deliberate and why. A count with a note preserves the number and loses the argument.

#232 read all twelve by hand: about nine are real extractable duplication, two are `LibraryBook` and `BookRecord` sharing a field vocabulary across the adapter boundary, and one is `floors.ts`'s `unarmedState` and `capUnarmedState`, which a spec calls the ratchet mirrored.

deliberate-ignore-comments.why: A `jscpd:ignore-start` and `jscpd:ignore-end` pair marks an intentional clone where it lives, with a comment beside it that says why. The reason sits next to the code, rather than in a baseline document that drifts away from it.
rel: The directive moves the clone count and the total-line denominator together, so nothing sees it unless something counts it.
#237 session, jscpd 5.0.16: a 34-line file with a 12-line ignore block reported 20 lines, and the pair reported 32 of 46 raw lines with 0 clones
notes: Read this cell with the Watching row. On its own the directive is G38's failure shape and G43's directive shape at once: it takes lines out of the numerator and the denominator together, from inside a source file, nowhere near any file a deploy reads.

`--ignore-pattern` does not do this job and must not be reached for. Its help text reads like region suppression. Measured: a `// cpd-disable` line above the clone changed nothing, and the clone still reported. It skips tokens that match a regex.
The measurement corrected an overclaim on the way. An earlier reading said the whole file leaves the analysis. It does not. A file's live lines still count, and only the ignored region leaves.

deliberate-tune.why: The intentional clones here are short. A higher token threshold drops them without any annotation in the source.
rel: One threshold step that drops intentional clones also drops real ones; the same step moved 82 clones to 12.
#232 — the identical tree read 2.51% at 20/3 and 0.51% at 50/5
notes: The ticket already named the risk: a measure tuned until it stops complaining is a measure that stopped measuring. That is a reason to refuse rather than to tune.

deliberate-nothing.why: The series refuses nothing, so nobody must agree in advance about what the number includes. A reader judges each clone when they look.
rel: A cap needs a stated rule for what the number holds, or its refusal has no agreed meaning.
notes: Nothing in this box rules it out under the chosen set. It differs from the chosen cell only in whether the intentional clones are named once in writing.
The reason to name them anyway: the first reader who meets 12 clones and no note re-derives the by-hand reading #232 already did.

population-scoped-union.why: One jscpd run over the eight scope globs together, with test files dropped. Each clone counts in every scope it touches. The run sees a clone whose halves sit in different scopes.
rel: A clone counted in two scopes makes the eight numbers non-additive, so the totals must be per scope.
notes: The cost, recorded rather than hidden: the eight numbers no longer sum to a repository total. A cross-scope clone appears twice by construction.

The gap this closes is latent today and not hypothetical. #232 measured the combined run at 12 clones and 133 duplicated lines, and the eight per-scope runs sum to exactly the same. The two agree now, so the switch costs nothing and closes the hole before it opens.
The population rule is complexity spec §2 verbatim: one glob per scope, minus *.test.ts, with the exclusions list not applied and excludedDirectories not read.

population-scoped-separate.why: Eight independent runs, one per scope, exactly as the complexity counter walks its populations. The eight numbers sum to a repository total.
rel: Separate runs cannot see a clone spanning two scopes, which is the failure duplication exists to catch.
#232 — jscpd matches across files by construction, and its per-scope and combined runs agree only because no cross-scope clone exists today
notes: It is the option that matches every other series in this repository, and that is a real argument for it. The counter-argument is a domain fact: complexity is a property of one function, and a clone is a relation between two places.
A relation does not partition into scopes. That sentence is the whole of why this row is not settled by consistency.

population-plus-gates.why: gates/ is 42 files of load-bearing code that no complexity series watches. The complexity spec keeps it on an override list as a candidate population.
rel: gates/ is far more sensitive to the threshold than the source scopes, so its number is meaningless unstamped.
#232 — gates/ read 4 clones and 0.47% at 50/5, then 119 clones and 7.71% at 20/3, a 30x jump against 5x over the source scopes
notes: #232 checked the feared false positive and it is not there at the tool's defaults. All four clones in gates/ are import boilerplate or shared fixture construction, and none is an assertion.
This overlaps #239, which is live in another session and owns the test-code population question. This box defers to it and decides nothing about test files.

population-whole-tree.why: One jscpd run over the repository, one set of numbers, no scope label at all. It is the shape the tool produces without configuration.
rel: At jscpd's defaults, 570 of 1,042 duplicated lines are JSON this repository did not write.

#237 session, whole tree: 414 files, 91,435 lines, 74 clones, 1,042 duplicated lines (1.14%). The JSON row alone is 26 clones and 570 lines (10.88%), and reading them names cached provider responses in fixtures/api/ and the provisioned Grafana dashboard
Caps are keyed by scope in the floors file, armed or not, so a single repository number has no entry to hang on.
scripts/lib/floors.ts — parseCaps is called per scope name
notes: The argument against this cell used to be that it reads code no scope declares, which is the opposite of G38's rule. That edge was weak and it is replaced. Reading everything means nothing can silently leave the measurement, which is more fail-closed than a declared list, not less.

What refutes it is the measurement. `fixtures/api/oreilly-isbn-hit.json` and `fixtures/api/oreilly-search-hit.json` are 105 identical lines, because one book comes back from two endpoints. That is a fact about O'Reilly's API and not about this codebase, and it has no remedy: de-duplicating a recorded response falsifies the fixture.
It keeps the property the owner wanted. The TypeScript-only variant keeps that property without the data files.

watching-counted.why: `stryker.floors.json` gains a second per-population counter beside `ignored`. A gate sweeps scoped source for the directive and compares the two. The nightly job knows its own commit, so it generates the links at the moment it emits.
rel: A declared count needs a defined population, or the sweep and the declaration count different files.
notes: This is G43 applied to a second tool, and G43's own file is the argument for it. It says a Stryker disable directive is the one route down that leaves no trace in either file the deploy reads, and it closes that at merge rather than at deploy, because `required_approving_review_count: 0` leaves the gate suite as the only pre-merge surface there is. Every word transfers.

`countDisableDirectives` is the working shape to copy: a regex that requires a comment opener immediately before the directive word, attributed to the first scope whose glob matches, over-matching on purpose because a missed directive is silent and a false positive is a red build somebody reads.

Its own comment records a trap worth inheriting. Widening that pattern once made the module's prose count itself, so the directive forms are described in the source and spelled only in a spec file that no scope reads.

Record the ignored line count as a fourth number, not only the block count. A declared block still shrinks the denominator, so without it the pre-suppression total is unrecoverable and a suppression still shows up as nothing.

watching-stored-links.why: Each declared block carries a permanent link to the code it covers, so a reviewer reads the actual clone from the pull request instead of taking a count on trust.
rel: A stale link that still resolves reads as current, so a reviewer approving a cap-clearing block reads the wrong code.
notes: The goal is right and the storage is what fails. A permanent link pins a commit, so it never breaks and never updates. A stale link that still resolves reads as current, which is silence that looks like health.

Nothing here can check that a link resolves. G21 records any request the suite makes and fails the test that made it. So a stored link is shape-checked only, which AGENTS.md already calls a typo guard and explicitly not a correctness guarantee, about the frontmatter contributor ids.
G43's own file declined a note-presence check for the neighbouring reason: any string satisfies it, so it catches the honest omission and not the adversary.

watching-labels.why: Put the file and line of each block into the recorded series as labels, so the dashboard lists them with no second file to keep true.
rel: Pushgateway never forgets a series, so a block that moves line mints a new one and the old draws a confident flat line.
docs/spec/gate-or-trend.md §2 — Pushgateway strips timestamps by construction and never forgets a series, so a dead nightly draws a confident flat line
notes: Every ignore block that moves leaves a permanent ghost. That is the exact failure the trend layer names as its own characteristic one.

watching-none.why: The number refuses nothing while every cap is unarmed, so an unwatched directive costs a distorted line rather than a bypassed refusal.
rel: An unarmed cap plans to arm, and an unwatched directive is the cheapest route around it on the day it does.
#237 session — the directive moves numerator and denominator together, leaving no diff in any file a deploy reads
notes: It is survivable only while nothing ever arms. This repository already carries a gate whose whole existence is the same directive on a different tool.

population-whole-tree-ts.why: jscpd's `--format` flag restricts the scan to TypeScript. The whole tree is read, so no declaration list can shrink the population, and the JSON and Markdown that swamped the whole-tree run leave by file type.
rel: It still has no scope key, so a cap in the floors file has no entry to hang on.
scripts/lib/floors.ts — parseCaps is called per scope name
notes: Measured in the same run: 190 files, 45,869 lines, 35 clones, 363 duplicated lines, 0.79%. Against the eight declared scopes at 94 files, 25,999 lines, 12 clones, 133 lines, 0.51%.
The 23 extra clones are test and gate files. That forces an answer to #239, which owns the test-code population question and is live in another session. This box does not answer it.

population-scoped-plus-whole.why: Two readings from one tool. The eight declared scopes carry the numbers a cap hangs on. One whole-tree TypeScript number sits beside them, and no declaration list can shrink it.
rel: Two populations means two sets of counts, and both need the same stamped parameters.
A block in a file no scope declares is invisible to a per-scope sweep, so the sweep follows the wider population.
notes: It answers the concern behind the whole-tree proposal without paying its measured cost. The blind spot the owner was closing is real: `gates/` and the top of `packages/site/src` are read by no scope.
The cost is one more number and one more panel. The whole-tree number is never capped, because it holds test and gate code that #239 has not ruled on.
Within the eight, the run is still one scan rather than eight, so a clone whose halves sit in two scopes is seen. It counts in both, and the eight therefore do not sum.

teeth-arm-now.why: The baseline exists already, so a cap could be set from it on the first run and the calibration window skipped.
rel: A cap set before the parameters are stamped compares two numbers that need not mean the same thing.
docs/spec/complexity-on-the-trend-layer.md §4 — a record stamped under a different counting rule is refused rather than compared
notes: The complexity ratchet refuses this by construction. A cap is the highest value observed across a twenty-run window, and arming is a human judgement made per scope after that window fills.
One measurement is not a level. #232's baseline was taken on one tree on one day, and nothing yet says whether 133 duplicated lines is this repository's normal or its best day.

suspected: A pre-commit hook that prints the duplication a commit adds would shift this left, as CRAP already does. It is not an edge because no option here is a hook, and the complexity spec already put the hook question to bed for its own metric.

An eslint-disable-next-line complexity comment appears able to drop a function from the shipped complexity population silently, in the same shape measured for jscpd:ignore-start. Filed as #244. Read rather than run, so it colours nothing here.

presets.title: As recommended
presets.text: The chosen set is Claude's recommendation, not the owner's decision. Open the two rows that carry the argument.

presets.title: Cap it after all
presets.text: The strongest reason not to cap. Turn the cap on, then allow the ignore directive, and read the conflict.

presets.title: Adopt nothing
presets.text: The strawman the map calls a first-class result. Select it and see what switches off.

presets.title: The break test
presets.text: Change the most connected chosen cell. Record the percentage instead of counts, and read what moves.

presets.title: The owner's set
presets.text: The three cells the owner proposed, before the whole-tree measurement. Read the population row last.

presets.title: Watch nothing
presets.text: Allow the ignore directive and count nothing. This is the configuration the measurement was taken against.
